Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, I have allocated 1 minute to each honorable member to speak in today's National Assembly meeting. First, Honorable Member Goma Devi Timalsina.
Honorable Member Goma Devi Timalsina (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honorable Chairperson, the public is forced to travel at risk. People are facing immense hardship in places like Munglin-Narayangadh, BP Highway, Roshi River. Similarly, in hilly areas like Doti, Baitadi, accidents are happening almost daily. The government has not paid attention to this. The government's attention is focused on trivial matters like evicting the landless. I would like to state that the government's attention should be drawn to such positive matters, and I conclude, thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Durga Gurung.
Honorable Member Durga Gurung (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, today through the esteemed National Assembly, I want to raise the issue of road transport problems faced by the citizens of Karnali Province during the monsoon. Every year, as soon as the monsoon begins, roads in various districts of Karnali are obstructed due to landslides, floods, and road blockages. This has seriously affected the daily life, health services, education, transportation of agricultural produce, and emergency rescue operations of the local citizens. In some places, patients have even lost their lives due to not receiving timely treatment. Although Karnali is a part of Nepal, it is lagging behind in terms of road infrastructure. Therefore, to minimize road blockages during the monsoon, sustainable and quality road construction, landslide control, timely maintenance, and emergency equipment are necessary. (Time expired.)
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Nar Bahadur Bisht.
Honorable Member Nar Bahadur Bisht (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honorable Chairperson, a Force vehicle going from Surkhet to Kalikot met with an accident in the Dailekh section. Some say 14 passengers, some say 9, the exact number is unclear, and so far 3 have been identified. The driver and co-driver are two brothers from the same family in Puthari Municipality. I would like to offer my heartfelt condolences to the deceased and urge that the search operation continue immediately. On the other hand, what is the government's stance on the upcoming floods and landslides? I would like to draw the attention of the Home Ministry, through the Honorable Chairperson, to inform the House about this as soon as possible. Because floods and landslides are occurring in many places, and incidents are also happening frequently. What are the preparations for that? I would like to receive information about that, thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Narayan Dutt Mishra.
Honorable Member Narayan Dutt Mishra (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, has the government purchased DAP fertilizer at a high price? This is the question. Is it true that India purchased DAP fertilizer from the same supplier for $540 and Nepal purchased the same fertilizer for $900 per metric ton, meaning $360 more? My question is, how did such a large difference occur in the purchase price between India and Nepal? Was fair competition held during the purchase? Given the price difference of almost double, should an investigation be conducted? What is the government's plan? On one hand, there is a severe shortage of fertilizer across the country, and on the other hand, it is certain that even with expensive purchases, less fertilizer will arrive. If this is the case, how transparent will the purchase of 3 billion worth of vehicles be? This is also a pressing question for the government.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Yuvraj Sharma.
Honorable Member Yuvraj Sharma (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, the Melamchi water distribution has been stopped again. Health and education taxes have increased. The government's talk of restructuring health insurance will be in vain. The number of people renewing health insurance seems to be decreasing further. Honorable Chairperson, similarly, in many places across the country, shops selling gutkha, tobacco, and alcohol are operating freely within 300 meters of schools. I want to ask if the government should regulate this. Honorable Chairperson, Kathmandu Metropolitan City and community schools in the western Terai cannot be compared. The policy and program budget for FY 2083/084 does not seem very successful in this regard either. The narrative distorted by party politics is also not entirely correct. Educated parents and subject teachers are needed. The heavy bags of students and the examination system are equally to blame. The nation needs education and schools, not just schools. The education system from a century ago by Light Macaulay... (Time expired.)

Honorable Member Suresh Kumar Ale Magar.
Honorable Member Suresh Kumar Ale Magar (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honorable Chairperson, although I did not speak during the zero hour, I will speak on this. Honorable Chairperson, I want to say a few things about the "Prevention of Money Laundering (Third Amendment) Bill, 2083" presented by the Honorable Minister of Finance with a message from the House of Representatives. I wanted to find out, I have been trying to find out. While stating this, regarding this bill, what I feel is that money laundering, washing money, making black money white money. This is indeed a crime. It is true that some of our journalist friends are not aware of this. That's why our respected leader, Honorable Bishnu Poudel, was repeatedly asked by journalists if he opposed money laundering. He said that since it is a crime, it should be opposed. That's how it was. Therefore, this thing, this is a crime.
Money laundering is a crime. The law that was made regarding its prevention was brought in this context. The government has brought this because some amendments were felt necessary in this law. In the existing Money Laundering Prevention Act, upon a cursory review, two amendments and one new provision have been made in section 64. I believe that the government, which has come with the mandate of the people and with a vast majority, has brought this after careful consideration. In this sense, from what I have seen cursorily in this bill, in the ordinance, I feel that it is not entirely wrong. However, Honorable Chairperson, whether any policy, any law is right or wrong depends on its implementation, and its implementation depends on the intention and honesty of the implementer. Therefore, looking from this angle, I would like to give the government the benefit of the doubt at this time. I believe that this amendment has been brought with good intentions and will be implemented accordingly, and I hope that this government will do something different from the previous governments. In that sense, I think it would be appropriate to take this bill, which has been brought by establishing this ordinance, through the necessary process. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri.
Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, while participating in the discussion on this anti-money laundering, this property purification related ordinance, there are two things. Rather than the content, I am opposing the process of discussion. Bringing an ordinance by convening parliament and then circumventing parliament is a wrong practice, regardless of which government brings it, I want to say that. And I want to find out what the content is. Beyond the content, what is happening is that under the Property Purification Act, currently, police offices are also being given permission for initial investigation. In a case, a person apprehended in one incident is being apprehended and the process of opening a property purification case against them is also there, and it seems that its practice is not right. How can this be managed? That's one thing. Similarly, the current Rastriya Swatantra Party chairman Rabi Lamichhane had cases of cooperative fraud, money laundering, and other organized crimes against him, filed by the previous government. Now, as Nepal is falling into the grey list, according to the FATF, his cases are being withdrawn one after another from the court. So, what is this double standard? This also needs attention. Therefore, this issue, is it that Ravi...

Lamichhane, is this government making this law to use other people, just like the previous government did? I want to raise this point, and I won't say much on other matters because I feel that instead of rushing this through the full house, the assembly house, it should be taken to a committee for some discussion. We also want to provide some input on the content. Because we want this law to be good, and we want to use legislative authority and legislative wisdom in the right way. Therefore, I want to say this.

When responding in the House of Representatives, the Honorable Finance Minister had said, "Previous governments used this asset purification as a weapon, they fined our Speaker, and they tried to investigate me too. Employees told me," he said publicly in the sovereign parliament. Which employees were investigated by the previous government, and which government told former MP Dr. Swarnim Wagle? Which employee leaked this information? And if what he said in such a public forum is true, then reveal that person and the government, and if it is not true, then stop the Finance Minister's outright lie. Apologize in a public ceremony, and I request that this be taken to a committee. This should be discussed in a committee, not in the full house. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Bishnu Kumari Sapkota.
(13:46 hrs)
Honorable Bishnu Kumari Sapkota (Nepali Congress): Honorable Chairperson,
(13:46 hrs)
Today, we are having a theoretical discussion on the bill to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2064. This amendment was also necessary for Nepal. However, looking at the points amended by the government in this bill, it feels like it is making it easier and broader for the convenience of the nation and citizens. More than the benefit, it is for the government.

Honorable Chairperson, the formal economy of Nepal is currently only 66 trillion GDP, while more than 40 percent is an informal economy. Instead of the government investigating and bringing this into the legal framework, those who are already paying property tax under the government are being subjected to various troubles and harassment. What about those who have accumulated wealth secretly, evading the government? Is this government perhaps trying to trap democrats under one pretext or another?

Honorable Chairperson, in international practice, it is clearly stated with a specific amount how much tax citizens should pay on the wealth they earn and how much they do not have to pay. However, in our country, a system of paying tax based on estimation without investigation or monitoring is being forcibly imposed. This needs to be widely discussed, and a system of fixed tax based on a fixed amount, along with provisions for how much property one person can hold, should be included. For this, I want to draw the government's attention through the Honorable Chairperson to send this bill to the Legislation Management Committee for clause-by-clause discussion. Thank you. Jai Nepal.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Roshi Meche.
(13:48 hrs)
Honorable Roshi Meche (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Chairperson,
(13:49 hrs)
Sir, preventing money laundering and financial crimes should be a common national priority not just for a single party or government, but for the entire state. We need a strong legal structure to save the country from the international standards of the Grey List. There is no doubt about this. However, in the name of making the law strict, the established principles of criminal justice, procedural justice, and institutional balance should not be narrowed. I see a need for serious reconsideration of some practical and theoretical aspects of the amendment brought through this bill. I want to draw the attention of this honorable house mainly to three policy aspects.

First: Jurisdictional Conflict and Institutional Ambiguity. In our state system, bodies established to regulate and investigate specialized sectors like tax, banking, securities, and insurance are already active. This amendment may open the door for the Asset Purification Investigation Department to directly enter all related offenses in these sectors. This can create serious jurisdictional disputes between established regulators and the department, risking further ambiguity in the system instead of strengthening the investigation. To prevent such ambiguity, a clear legal framework for inter-agency coordination is necessary.

Second: Risk-Based Investigation and Optimal Use of Resources. Asset purification investigation is a very complex and resource-intensive process. Applying this strict law to minor or technical financial errors can lead to wasteful expenditure of the state's limited resources and create unnecessary fear among small businesses. Therefore, for serious offenses like organized crime or corruption, a certain minimum threshold should be set so that the department can focus its energy only on high-risk and strategic areas.

Third: Prosecution Without Predicate Offense and Risk of Arbitrariness. The most sensitive aspect is the provision that allows prosecution for asset purification even when the predicate offense is not proven or a case has not even been filed. The established principle of asset purification is that the predicate offense must be proven first. Granting the autonomy to prosecute without a predicate offense can increase arbitrary state control over citizens' property rights and business freedom, and there is a high risk of its misuse. Strong safeguards are essential in the bill to prevent such a trend. Chairperson Sir, only a just and balanced law strengthens the state system. Therefore, I strongly demand that this bill should not be passed in its current form hastily, but should be moved forward only after thorough deliberation with financial experts and stakeholders, with clear amendments to prevent potential risks. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson: Honorable Member Khamma Bahadur Khalti.
(13:51 hrs)
Honorable Khamma Bahadur Khalti (Nepali Congress): Honorable Chairperson, I am expressing my views today focusing only on limited clauses. This appears contrary to the preamble. Number 1: The ordinance is contrary to Article 194(2)(c) of the Constitution. It should only be brought in case of such urgency. A replacement bill has come through an ordinance, and I see that it has been done in a bit of a hurry. Therefore, the preamble states that it is desirable to make legal provisions regarding the prevention of money laundering from criminal activities and the financing of terrorist activities, hence the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2064 was enacted. However, looking at the content of clause 13(1)(c) and then clause 22(1) of the current bill, it appears to override other existing laws and regulations on specific subjects. Looking at this, it seems to affect and override other special laws in the context of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act and is out of jurisdiction. I want to draw the attention of the concerned government through the Honorable Chairperson to this matter. Therefore, we must also pay special attention to the situation before this amendment. All laws have their own objectives, and therefore, regarding the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, I would like to point out the provision of clause 27, the provision for suspension. While the clause of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act remains as it is, the regulation of the House of Representatives has been passed, and in the case of Ravi Lamichhane, there is a context of withdrawing the case. The Office of the Attorney General decides whether to file or withdraw a case. Delegating that power, government lawyers file cases, and in the context of cases that have already been filed, the process is being reopened even though the law has not been amended. The government should not have such a mindset and perspective of withdrawing or filing cases. In my opinion and perspective, this weakens the institution.

Another important matter is that in the context of money laundering, we cannot ignore the cases of Sudan Gurung and Deepak Bhat. Even though a permanent institution exists, a committee was formed against it, and he was reinstated as Home Minister, which has not been made public. Therefore, to ensure that one law does not override another, I want to draw the government's attention through the Honorable Chairperson to send this to the Legislation Committee for detailed discussion. Thank you. Jai Nepal.

Second point, regarding the cases related to money laundering, whom is the government trying to prosecute by bringing these bills? The case of the ruling party's chairman has been withdrawn. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, received with a message from the House of Representatives (13:58 PM) "Consideration of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Third Amendment) Bill, 2083" is now concluded. Honorable members, the turn of honorable members to speak in the discussion is now over. Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Minister of Finance, Dr. Swarnim Wagle, to respond to the questions raised in the discussion. Honorable Minister of Finance Dr. Swarnim Wagle:- Honorable Chairperson, honorable members, I have taken note of the issues raised by you. I wish to briefly answer your queries and questions. I would like to thank Honorable Member Suresh Ale Magar for expressing his intention that the issue of money laundering is criminal, serious, and that the government should provide the benefit of asset purification. Indeed, that is its essence. If we fail to act, we will be blacklisted, and being blacklisted means all our financial relations with the rest of the world will be severed. We need to attract remittances, attract foreign direct investment in such important matters, and enhance our international reputation and credibility. If we fail to perform our duties, which are essentially regular state obligations and regular governance practices, we are at high risk of falling to the level of countries like Haiti and Somalia. We are trying to erase this from February 2081. I would also like to inform the honorable house that significant progress has been made in the 40 days since we took office. We have been given 15 urgent action plans by the Financial Action Task Force, with instructions to work on these specific areas. Out of these 15, zero were fully addressed, and zero were substantially addressed. Six were partially addressed, and nine points were not addressed at all when we came into government. Since we took office, in the latest review, we have increased the number of fully addressed points from zero to three. We have reduced the number of partially addressed points from six to four, and the number of points not addressed at all has been reduced from nine to eight. However, by holding another meeting of the relevant committee next week and setting milestones, and by activating all state mechanisms, we will bring these eight points to the category of almost all addressed or fully addressed at once, and we are working with that urgency. Therefore, if you actually look at the context of this sense of urgency, there is not much. There are two simple amendments, and a lengthy discussion is not deemed necessary. Honorable members, you wanted to go into the content, and you should go into the content. What are the contents? What are your constructive suggestions, intellectual suggestions, and practical suggestions for amendment? I would like to humbly request the honorable members to pay attention to them, as the former Attorney General has made some good suggestions for improvement, which I have noted. Now, regarding the intention, why the ordinance was brought, it is based on the provisions written in the constitution. The main thing is to look at the intention. Efforts were made earlier to split parties and other malicious attempts, but that is not the focus. We are working with the objective of getting the country out of the gray list as soon as possible. The state itself must be involved in this, and we have moved forward with the expectation of the state's cooperation, and I hope for cooperation from the honorable house, both houses, the lower house and the upper house, in the same spirit. In the past, there was revenge, but now revenge should not be excessive. In response to a question raised in the House of Representatives, I said that revenge should not be taken this time, as we are under international scrutiny. Gray list is a colloquial term; its technical name is Jurisdictions under Increased Scrutiny, meaning that the international community is exerting extreme pressure and scrutiny on our financial sector activities every second, and the Financial Action Task Force is doing so. If we deviate even slightly, they warn us. Therefore, we are especially cautious about the possibility of escaping the gray list if an act as powerful as money laundering is misused for political purposes. Therefore, I will not go into what happened when such a body was kept under the direct control of the Prime Minister in the past. This time, it must be done differently, in a purely professional manner and with professionalism, and therefore it has been kept under the Ministry of Finance. I receive its professional briefing, and we are working with the decision not to proceed against anyone without irrefutable evidence. Therefore, I made the point that the era of revenge is over. Regarding the naming of some individuals, we should not delve into court matters. The name of our party president also came up. I hope that the previous government will take responsibility for the decisions made by the previous government, and I do not think it is appropriate to second-guess matters that have already been decided by the court within the parliamentary dignity. Issues of small economic matters and large matters were raised. I feel we need to be a bit clearer about the technical understanding of money laundering. I mentioned in the House of Representatives that if someone earns money and wants to use it out of envy or malice, or to achieve political objectives against someone, they might think of applying money laundering, using this weapon, and misusing state resources. We have moved far beyond such unpleasant practices. What we need to be clear about now is that money laundering is a second-degree crime. First, if someone has acquired illicit wealth through smuggling, trafficking, or corruption, that must first be established. The first-degree crime must be established, and money laundering is applied only to the activity carried out in the second stage to legitimize the proceeds from that crime. Therefore, it is not about applying it to someone if they are disliked, as is the common saying, and we want to work faithfully and loyally towards international recognition. Therefore, let's establish predicate offenses. There are 13 bodies in Nepal for investigation, from customs to revenue to the CIAA to CIB. They have been doing these works based on 50 different laws. However, matters not covered by them, especially those related to economic crimes, are currently under judicial review, the largest financial crime in Nepal's history. An investigation is ongoing based on claims of over one trillion. If we do not present such bold decisions with political courage to get out of the FATF, we will not get out of the gray list. Because the FATF essentially says that you make laws, you write everything that needs to be written, you try to blind us with dust at the same time, but you do not implement them. How many cases have been filed? How many assets have been confiscated? What is the training on seizures? What is the state's capacity? We are now facing scrutiny on such matters. What is being attempted now is also in that direction. We are moving towards implementing some laws and regulations with strictness and regularity so that we can quickly remove this stigma from our nation. My attention has been drawn to the issue raised by Honorable Khamma Bahadur Khati, but the scope of the amendment is small. When the ordinance was brought, we showed such promptness to project this sense of urgency. If it is my personal wish, we should create a super authority related to economic crimes to further empower these 13 investigation and prosecution bodies, and there should be adequate public debate on it. If we see duplication, and a case taken forward from one place being reduced from another, we are very serious about the risks of politicization and consolidation. However, if you look at the context of today's ordinance or this replacement bill, it is very narrow, focused, and has a time-limited purpose, so I do not see many risks or loopholes opening up from it. Finally, regarding the issue raised by Honorable Somnath Adhikari, why the ordinance was brought, this is a bit old now. We have already given a satisfactory answer to it. It was brought based on the constitutional provision that allows bringing ordinances. The main thing is the intention. The intention is clear and pure. Thank you. (14:14 hrs) Honorable Mr. Basudev Ghimire (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, the ordinance brought by bypassing this parliament appears to be of wrong intention and self-serving. The bill to amend the 'Some Nepal Laws related to Health Sciences Institute' to replace it seems to have been brought through the old method and procedure. Although, now there is a lot of propaganda and... because our current government is in power, we have to pass it, and they will pass it so that they can work, however, this is not a good practice, and good governance is not being done, I conclude my brief statement. Thank you, Jai Nepal. Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable Member Meenasingh Rakhal. (14:16 hrs) 97 Honorable Mr. Meenasingh Rakhal (Nepal Communist Party, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, the main objective of the Health Sciences Amendment Bill is to improve service and quality, establish good governance, and accountability. However, merely by adjusting the tenure of office bearers or amending the administrative committee, the real problems in the health sector will not be solved. Nepal B.P. Koirala Health Sciences Institute, Pokhara Health Sciences Institute, Rapti Health Sciences Institute, and Karnali Health Sciences Institute, among others, have been established. Although the acts related to these institutes are in implementation, citizens have not been able to receive quality, accessible, and affordable health services as expected. Today, jokes are made on social media, those who score 23 get pass, those who score 24 get fail. Such comments are being made regarding qualifications, transparency, and impartiality in the health sector. If merit, access, and influence dominate appointments, promotions, and leadership, the very purpose of the institute will be weakened. Especially, the health situation in Karnali is challenging. The lack of specialist doctors, shortage of skilled manpower, inadequate management of equipment and medicines, weak physical infrastructure, remote geography, and lack of access to effective health insurance mean that citizens have to suffer greatly even for ordinary treatment. Therefore, this amendment should not only address the tenure of office bearers but also make health institutions more responsible, transparent, and accountable. Regulation is necessary, but emphasizing absolute regulation in a way that weakens the self-reliant character of cooperatives is not theoretically correct. The division of work related to cooperatives between the federal, provincial, and local levels, as granted by the constitution, should be clear in the bill. Cooperatives should be made the basis of economic prosperity by linking them with production, entrepreneurship, and employment. The bill should have clear theoretical definitions on matters such as minimum investment in the production sector, the role of cooperatives in agriculture, industry, tourism, small enterprises, and the role of youth and women returning from abroad, providing entrepreneurship loans through cooperatives, developing value chains, creating production and employment, and promoting digital governance and transparency. The pullist thinking of this bill, which aims to bring loans from abroad and give them to depositors, is not sufficient to meet the needs of cooperatives.

Mr. Speaker, Sir, while enacting laws, it is necessary not only to address the problems seen in the cooperative sector at present but also to consider the future problems that may arise. This bill needs to be sent to the legislative committee for further extensive discussion, incorporating the suggestions of experts and stakeholders, before it can be finalized. The issues incorporated in the bill do not seem to consider the legislative act. In conclusion, cooperatives are not just institutions for collecting savings; they are a pillar of production, employment, entrepreneurship, and the local economy, and even the national economy. Therefore, it is necessary to take this bill to the legislative committee for discussion and amendment to fulfill the goals of production-oriented employment and a socialist-oriented economy. Thank you, greetings.

Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member Somnath Poudel.
(3:07 PM)
34
Honorable Mr. Somnath Poudel (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honorable Speaker, Sir, I seek permission to present my views in the discussion on the bill to amend the Cooperative Act, 2074, 2083 BS.
Today is International Cooperative Day. I extend my best wishes to all cooperative workers who work day and night to improve the living standards of citizens through cooperatives. Some aspects of this bill are naturally good, and we must preserve them. There are also some issues and questions in it. Therefore, I would like to request that this be discussed extensively. For example, one of the issues is that a member borrowing from a cooperative should not have to pay more than double the interest. Will this issue lead to timely repayment of loans taken from cooperatives? It doesn't seem like it will. Perhaps it was made with oneself in mind? It is also being discussed that the Speaker has a significant loan from the cooperative. The finalization of the case might take another 10-20 years. If they are allowed to charge any interest, then they will have to pay a large sum. It seems like this has been brought to protect the Speaker, by stating that one should not have to pay more than double. Therefore, I believe that this issue needs more discussion.

Sometimes, when laws are made, they are not just to solve today's problems. We must also address future issues and problems that may arise. However, this bill seems to be only for solving immediate problems. Therefore, it is necessary to think about this in a more long-term perspective. Hence, if we are to bring about overall reform in the cooperative sector and develop it as an institution that the public can trust, then, as many honorable members have said, it should be passed after extensive discussions with all stakeholders, and it should be sent to the relevant committee for clause-by-clause discussion. Thank you.

Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri.
(3:09 PM)
Honorable Mr. Ram Kumari Jhankri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Speaker, Sir, this Cooperative Act, 2074 was amended through an ordinance, and I would like to raise two or three points while discussing this replacement bill. The issue of the ordinance coming again has already been raised. If this amendment had come, then so many things would have needed to be amended in the cooperative sector. The law would have required necessary modifications. There are some amendments in about 50 points. How much we can do with this, or how the government and this honorable house will view it, remains to be seen. Regarding the issue of cooperatives, the principle is that cooperatives are based on self-regulation. Self-regulation refers to the chain of production, consumption, and distribution, and it is only among members. That is what is meant by self-regulation. Many cooperatives were opened in our country, primarily for savings and loans, and the regulatory body, the Cooperative Department, became extremely weak. As a result, now there is even an authority. This has led to numerous problems and social malpractices. For instance, the IMF has repeatedly told the Government of Nepal to formalize the large amount of money in the non-formal economy and has issued many circulars. Consequently, cooperatives have become a somewhat unpleasant topic for everyone to hear about. Therefore, we need to look at the principle of production, consumption, and distribution, and the creation of self-employment, from one perspective. And the aspect of regulating savings and loans needs to be viewed from another perspective. Issues like interest rates are different. And in the ordinance that has come now, specifically three or four things need to be amended. For example, the definition includes family members, which are prohibited by existing laws. These things make it seem as if it was brought with malicious intent. This is because the chairman of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, who is currently leading the government, is involved in this case, and he has not been acquitted from here. Although the case is sub judice, due to legal loopholes and policy gaps, people have six cases. Therefore, it is an opportunity for us to see if this issue is being misused. So, out of these 50 points, how many clauses are open? This remains to be seen. But if we get to discuss the content in the committee, we can point out some things, enhance this law, and incorporate our experiences, the experiences of experts, and the experiences of those who have worked in the field, as they know where the problems lie. Much work needs to be done in the context of cooperatives. Therefore, even if we try to pass this law today with some amendments from this house, since many clauses are open, I request that it be sent to the committee for discussion. Thank you.

Let's discuss. That is our input.
36
Honorable Speaker: Honorable members, the discussion on the proposal to consider the Cooperative First Amendment Bill, 2083 BS, received with a message from the House of Representatives, will conclude here.
Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Minister of Land Management, Cooperatives, and Poverty Alleviation, Pratibha Rawal, to respond to the questions raised in the discussion.
Honorable Minister of Land Management, Cooperatives, and Poverty Alleviation, Mr. Pratibha Rawal: Honorable Speaker, Sir, I sincerely thank the honorable members for their valuable suggestions in the discussion on the ordinance brought to amend the Cooperative Act, 2074 BS. Since this was a theoretical discussion and clause-by-clause discussion will follow, I have also gained confidence that we will receive more of your advice and suggestions during the clause-by-clause discussion regarding why those clauses were included. Firstly, regarding cooperatives, we are all aware of the principles and spirit in which cooperatives were established and their current situation. That is why, while discussing cooperatives here, we must also address the pain of thousands of depositors whose savings have not been returned. This was the immediate need. That is why some knots have been untied, and as the honorable members have said, many things need to be amended. However, by untying some knots, such as the repayment of savings for small depositors starting after the ordinance was issued, much work needs to be done. But this was brought with the objective of providing some relief to them by starting something immediately. Some knots have been untied. However, much more reform is needed. I agree with this.

Similarly, regarding the issue of funds, there is also the issue of the definition of family being made somewhat broad. However, as we complete 100 days today, based on our experience and work, it has become apparent that we need to be somewhat strict regarding loans and directors in cooperatives, otherwise, it is not possible to recover money easily. Currently, the trend observed is that family members and relatives of cooperative members are involved, and they themselves are engaged in it. Therefore, based on our experience, we have found that the definition of family needs to be made somewhat broader. I would like to inform the honorable members that this definition of family has been elaborated.

Similarly, the issue of funds was also raised. How is the fund being managed? There was also a suggestion from an honorable member that this should be discussed in the committee. The procedure for the fund, passed by our cabinet, has been published in the Gazette on 2083/1/10. I kindly request the honorable members to look at it and provide your feedback. We will wholeheartedly welcome it because you are our seniors and experienced. Therefore, if you have any suggestions regarding that procedure, even if you submit them in writing, we will proceed according to your suggestions and are ready to make it work. Because we are not in a situation to rush things or proceed slowly. The cooperative is currently in a state where we need to get it out as quickly as possible. Some are very problematic, and some are heading towards problems. We need to prevent that, and regarding the grey list we are talking about, we need to be somewhat strict in some aspects of cooperative regulation. We need to be strict and firm in the regulation and supervision of cooperatives. Only then can we get out of the grey list. We have set criteria for this. Therefore, we are working on it. Also, the issue of banks not being allowed to conduct transactions with cooperative banks and unions, and the possibility of this being done illegally or attempted this year, was raised by honorable members.

One more thing, regarding the special investigation committee that was formed for our cooperatives. As we are making changes to the clauses today and untying some knots, I would like to inform you that we have held discussions with all relevant stakeholders, and by holding sufficient discussions, some knots have been untied. These provisions have been made today.

For example, we have drafted this after consulting with cooperative victims, those depositors who are currently in pain, as well as the Nepal Rastra Bank, CIB, the Attorney General's Office, and four other counting institutions. We have taken their suggestions. Along with that, the suggestions given in the report of the special investigation committee have also been incorporated into this amendment. Therefore, at that time, I felt or that

While presenting the report, which is 1100 pages long, if the suggestions in it were actually followed at the time when the report was presented to the House of Representatives, accepted by the House of Representatives, and ordered by the government for implementation. If the things written in that report were followed literally, perhaps today the cooperatives or all of this would not have happened because it is not a problem that arose overnight, nor is it a problem that can be solved overnight. But some improvement-oriented work could have been done at that time. They have suggested some policy reforms in the law. If we had implemented the suggestions from that report at that time, we could have made some improvements in the cooperative sector, and we could have prevented the problem from escalating as much as it has now. That is my realization and understanding while looking at that report. And earlier, many things, like the issue of our party chairman, also came up. Especially, your advice and suggestions, because this assembly is an assembly of experts, we are much junior to you and have to learn from your experience after coming to this assembly. Therefore, suggestions from here are more important to us than discussions in other committees. That's why tomorrow, in the clause-by-clause discussion, even if you propose amendments, as our minister also said earlier, we should present them in the clause-by-clause discussion. Because this law is being made in relation to the victims, without prejudice or bias, regardless of which party is involved, we will move forward by incorporating your valid suggestions and valid amendments. I also want to express my commitment from here. And a little bit now, I want to clarify about our chairman, when it comes to loans, regarding loan recovery, it is not allowed to take double the amount, and even now, some genuine borrowers are also victims of this. Therefore, it was necessary to untangle that knot, even if only to raise the issue. So, after connecting with the chairman's issue, an ordinance was issued some time ago, an ordinance to amend this cooperative. And what was the amendment in that issued ordinance? It was a provision that if the issue of cooperatives includes organized and money laundering issues, then reconciliation would not be possible. Therefore, if the honorable members had such suspicions, perhaps this clause would also have been amended, right? That's why I humbly request that there is no such prejudice or bias. It is not to fulfill anyone's vested interest. Therefore, let's move forward in a fast-forward manner to return the savings of the pure depositors. Let's be clear about the issue of recovering loans. That is the only objective. After this, in the clause-by-clause discussion, we will discuss openly on the amendments you have proposed. We will move forward by presenting what amendments are to be made. With that commitment, I conclude. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the proposal to consider the 'Cooperative First Amendment Bill, 2083', received with a message from the House of Representatives, will be concluded here. Honorable members, those who are in favor of this proposal will say 'Aye' and those who are against it will say 'No'. Honorable members in favor of this proposal will say 'Aye'. - 'Aye' Honorable members against this proposal will say 'No'. The sound of 'No' was not heard. Therefore, I declare that the proposal to consider the 'Cooperative First Amendment Bill, 2083', received with a message from the House of Representatives, has been unanimously approved. Honorable members, I would like to inform you that honorable members who wish to present amendment proposals on the 'Property Purification, Money Laundering Prevention Third Amendment Bill, 2083', the 'Health Science Academy Related Some Nepal Laws Amendment Bill, 2083', the 'Public Procurement Second Amendment Bill, 2083', and the 'Cooperative First Amendment Bill, 2083' can submit their amendment proposals to the legislative branch of the National Assembly in accordance with Rule 106 of the National Assembly Rules, 2075.
